paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Time dilation is a difference in how much time two clocks record. It can come from the clocks moving relative to each other, which is the special relativity version, or from the clocks sitting at places with different gravitational potential. When nobody says which, people usually mean the effect of speed. In special relativity, an observer measures a clock moving past them as ticking more slowly than a clock at rest beside them.

paragraphs.heading: Faster means slower
paragraphs.text: The greater the relative speed, the bigger the effect. As one clock gets close to the speed of light, 299,792,458 m/s, its time slows toward a stop. Because today's spacecraft are badly limited in speed, the gap people actually feel is tiny. An astronaut who spends 6 months on the International Space Station, circling Earth at about 7,700 m/s, ages about 5 milliseconds less than someone on the ground. The cosmonauts Sergei Krikalev and Sergey Avdeev both built up a difference of about 20 milliseconds.

paragraphs.heading: Why it happens
paragraphs.text: The effect follows from a basic rule of special relativity: light has the same speed for every observer. You cannot make light seem faster by moving toward its source or away from it, so the speeds of objects and of light do not simply add. Picture a clock whose ticks are timed by a pulse of light. When that clock moves past you, you see the pulse trace a longer, slanted path. To keep the speed of light the same, the time between ticks has to stretch, so the moving clock runs slow.

paragraphs.heading: Each sees the other slow
paragraphs.text: The effect works both ways. If a second observer rides along with the moving clock, each observer measures the other's clock as the slow one, since each sees the other as the one in motion. Common sense says a traveller whose time has slowed should see the outside world's time speed up, but special relativity predicts the opposite. A familiar comparison helps: two people looking at each other from far apart each see the other as small, and nobody calls that a contradiction.

paragraphs.heading: The twin paradox
paragraphs.text: This two-way effect leads to the twin paradox. One twin stays on Earth while the other goes on a space trip, and the symmetry seems to say they should be the same age when they meet again. In fact the traveller comes home younger. The puzzle goes away because the two situations are not alike: the twin at home stays in one frame of reference the whole time, while the traveller uses one frame going out and a different one coming back.

paragraphs.heading: Who saw it coming
paragraphs.text: Several writers predicted this slowing around the turn of the 20th century. In 1897 Joseph Larmor wrote that electrons in orbit take shorter times by the ratio √(1 − v²/c²), and in 1904 Emil Cohn tied that formula to the rate of clocks. Einstein showed in 1905 that the effect is about the nature of time itself, and he was the first to point out that it works both ways. Hermann Minkowski then introduced the concept of proper time in 1907, which made its meaning clearer.

paragraphs.heading: Real and useful
paragraphs.text: Experiments have confirmed these predictions again and again. They matter in practice too, for example in running satellite navigation systems such as GPS and Galileo. In principle, the effect would let passengers in a very fast vehicle reach the future in a short stretch of their own time. At high enough speed, one year of travel could match ten years on Earth.
